(in order of appearance):


1. It often features panels with speakers  (6)
2. Highly controlling? (8)
3. Something you may be willing to hold?  (6)(4)
4. Person who gets a lot of texts?  (4)(6)
5. Reflective post  (4)(6)


STEREO
PILOTING
ESTATE SALE
AVID READER
ROAD MARKER
Chevy Volt was a hybrid - not electric.  Chevy Bolt is the electric one.
Typical Monday. Nice and easy.

Cute Monday theme!


DIRNDL crossing DOUGIE was a tough cross for a Monday for this Boomer but I survived it. 🙂

If German "ach" is an ouburst, then so is English "oh." Examples: ach je (“heigh ho”), ach ja (“why, yes”), ach was (“by no means”), ach der (“oh, him”), ach so (“so I see”), ach nein (“you don’t mean…”), ach wo (“no way!” or “get out of here!”), ach wie schön (“oh, how lovely”), die ach so eingebildete Dame (“the oh so hoity-toity lady”).

Was humming along pretty well on acrosses only but even if I had gotten through to the bottom, ETHOS instead of ETHIC would have tripped me up (although maybe TOC isn’t a word for the down—but ASH is.) Then OLE before RAH and maybe POISON BREAK is a thing? What a Black WIDOW takes on vacation? But the DIRNDL and DOUGIE cross would have gotten me anyway. The only word I could think of for the down was BOUGIE. Once I let myself do all the downs I vaguely had a notion of DIRNDL from somewhere—so if not a Natick at least a Framingham. Pretty surprising cross for a Monday.

Loved this cute theme though. Tight!

Nice Monday, Chase, even if you're shooting for Tuesdays.
Thanks for the nod to my solving platform at 1A. 

A clue comment for the editors: if we're using borrow words like EID and DIRNDL, why not clue NORI as seaweed?
DIRNDL is a new one to me. Nice puzzle.

Never heard of ecru, supe, drindl or whatever the German dress was, dougie, fstop and had no idea when that song was in Les Mis nor have I seen Roman numerals in an answer before. What an insanely difficult corner for a Monday crossword.

What do you get when you cross Octoberfest garb with a 2010s dance craze?

An alphabet run on a Monday!
Came to grizzle over DIRNDL / DOUGIE  like a few others. Not only is it Monday, but Daylight Savings has just started here so it's unreasonably early to be hit with this 🥱
Is it the same STIEG Larson that makes the Far Side?
Also, I wonder if BOAs are worn with DIRNDLs when one is Oktoberfesting in SAO Paulo.

This was a delicious Monday romp. Had it been a dish served for dinner, and were I an adolescent, I would say A-RUB-ah-dub-dub Thanks for the grub! I happened to remember DIRNDL once the D and R were in, so I had no problem there ( DOUGIE wrote itself out from the crosses.) The real rub for me was the last to fall: ROTGUT. I had to look up what "hooch" is. Both clue and answer, two things I'd never heard of before. Conversely, two things I had indeed heard of before were MASSAGE and BLASÉ, two words I had *just* used, not even two hours before this puzzle dropped, in a reply to @dutchiris in the Sunday forum! Cue The Twilight Zone theme. — and most definitely cue ANITA Baker with "Giving You The Best That I Got," the song... https://youtu.be/8lbJgOJIS_8?is=L7hossot7CHWTKG6 ...or the full album (a lovely one for winding down from the weekend) https://youtube.com/playlist?list=OLAK5uy_m_FAUexJq5d909mIi3yads_Kln1LWZi5c&si=i941V9RHugD0EaJm

Everything went very quickly with this one, as Monday's should, and the only problem was the dance clue.  Fortunately, that was revealed by the crosses, because I didn't do so much fad dancing in the 2010s.

I know that dirndl skirts were a thing when I was a teenager, and I may even have had one. I don't remember what they looked like, but I think they were something Heidi wore in the Alps. Very folky and cute.

Thanks, Chase, for a dandy Monday.

"Phonetic spellings of alphabet letters will never be normal to me. Why are we using letters to spell words for other letters?"
- Because you gotta fill the grid with something, and when no actual words fit in we get delights such as phonetic spellings of alphabet letters...

How now, constructors?
Can we get themes on “mortal coil”, “soul of wit”, or “piece of work” next?

The amount of time I spent trying to rationalize "The rest, he rub." 

I was SO confused. And alarmed.

If the dougie could be danced at the Octoberfest, I suppose one could wear a drindl to dance in! Luckily the letter D is only the 4th letter in the alphabet to allow for a short alphabet run to figure out drindle dress crossing the dougie.

I'm surprise I haven't seen any outrage yet on SUPE for [Manager of an apt. bldg.]...

...IMO it's definitely borderline, at best.
This was challenging for me today
TUG clued under massage table was…interesting

No difficulty for me with this puzzle, though I did notice some words that were a bit unusual to see in a Monday puzzle. Some filled in with crosses, but most of them I knew anyway, 

Nice one, Chase.

Constructors and editors are kind, under most circumstances, about cluing archaisms as such (avid NYT cruciverbalists are accustomed to seeing  "obsolescent," "erstwhile," "one-time," or "... ,once" appear in at least a thousand clues a week on average). So, while it's never a tough get, I'm never going to cotton to seeing "RAH" clued as though it were a thing people still do.
Had to run the alphabet for the DIRNDL/DOUGIE  cross.  Pretty rare for a Monday. Took 12% more time than average to complete.
I knew Dirndl because King of the Hill references a nearby town called Dirndell! Never knew the dress had a specific name.

I rarely have to change anything in a Monday puzzle but today there were two such things: "ole" turned out to be RAH, and COWherd ended up being a COWHAND. RAH is one of the many common American words I find very weird, and remembering which just does not come naturally. Apparently it's short for hurrah? Many stadium cheers are international (I've screamed "Woo!!!" at the top of my lungs with crowds all over Europe), but not this.

LOLCAT! Now that's a blast from the past. It hasn't really been a thing for, what, 10 years? 15?

Sitting crosslegged is "sitting Turkish style" (siedzieć po turecku) in Polish. Teachers in kindergarten and elementary school required us to sit like that for long periods at a time. Apparently these days it's no longer practiced, and children are encouraged to change the positions they sit in, as it's healthier.

I guess "nonchalant" works as a clue for BLASE in a crossword, but personally I feel the words mean distinctly different things. I feel and act BLASE when I'm bored to death with something, or simply unimpressed by it, because it's just bleh, to me. I act nonchalantly when I don't care about something because I just don't feel the gravitas of the situation or don't care about the social mores being expressed. Polish people are often very serious, grave even, for the weirdest reasons, often inspired by conservative catholicism or a toxic caricature of patriotism, and nonchalance is my typical reaction to it.

What advice do you not get on a MASSAGE TABLE but i urge you to heed on a Monday morning??

Don’t look down!!

Yes, I succeeded with the Across Only challenge (ie not using any of the Down clues) although it took me a bit longer than usual — i took some wrong turns with RAH (“ole” — but PoISON BREAK is obviously not a thing) and ETHIC (i had “creed”) and WOMEN (i tried “in use” and “gents” — i suspect that isn’t used in America?) and SPARERIBS (I tried to shoehorn a “cajun” in there, stupidly). Also i could only picture Josephine Baker, but couldn’t remember her name! I guessed ANITA from the crosses. Yay me, eventually!

Happy Monday everyone!
THE SPOT TO RUB also partly works and threw me off

This one--one and done except for two little squares I had to check. Yea!!
 
*However,* can someone help me out with the Midi? How do 11A TONSOFFUN and 13A JONOSSOFF relate to 14D
[Result of walking a leadoff batter ... as seen in 11- and 13-Across?] ONEON? I'm flummoxed.  I see the word OFF in both, though. Is the title of the puzzle, Switch Positions, the key?
I understand that the DOUGIE is having a renaissance! Why? Because all the [ladies] love it!

@Sam – Thank you for that photo.  My whole being suddenly calmed down, getting the feel of those halcyon days back then, when things moved slower, and simple joys dominated life. Oh, that’s a fable, I know, but what a lovely fable to hang onto these days.  Plus, I smiled inside as well at how perfectly the photo fits the headline.
OTOE and TILT crossing ROTGUT, STIEG, and VOLT is not very monday. Ive never heard of any of the three downs!!
Beaten by a monday… beaten… what is a dirndl… i don’t know… it destroyed me

Chase had me at REPLETE, DIRNDL (a word hibernating in my brain for many years), and BLASÉ. BTW, if you, like me, are AT SEA regarding what the DOUGIE dance looks like, here: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/tWyelmgF4F8 . I’ve chronicled for ages how challenged I am at trying to guess the revealer from the theme answers, keeping it blank and not reading its clue. And, as usual, it’s been a long time since my last success, but that hasn’t stopped me from trying. Well. Today, after many LABORS, with a flash, a mighty flash, I suddenly saw that the theme answers involved rubbing. Then came another flash – “Could it be?”, “Could it be … THERE’S THE RUB?” Oh, this is going to be a very good day. Ain’t nothing going to dent it. Thank you, Chase!

In honour of SPAM, which might charitably be called a ‘hamlet’ and thus theme-adjacent, here is a link to a page from Florida State University with our famous Shakespearian source material undergoing some translational toing and froing, resulting in a processed item they call Spamlet: https://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/fun/spamlet/spamlet.html And a sample, after a trip to Esperanto and back: “Sleep - maybe dream: yes, here's the friction, Because in that sleepy sleep, what maybe dreams When we dragged this deadly bolt, It is necessary to give us a break.”

OTOE/STIEG, and DIRNDL/BOA (vs BRA)/DOUGIE was brutal no matter what day of the week.

A nice, easy puzzle until it wasn't.

Tough Monday for me. A number of things that were never going to dawn on me from the clues, so there was just a lot of working the crosses and pondering. No big deal. And.. puzzle find today - one of the more amazing I've ever stumbled on. A Sunday from October 7, 2018 by Tom McCoy with the title: "Mind the Gap." All of the theme answers included one square that was not actually part of the across answer. But... all of those answers actually kind of hinted at some kind of gap. Some examples (with the one square in parentheses): R(S)AILSPLITTER OUT(Q)ERSPACE RO(U)OMDIVIDER NA(A)SALCAVITY SECUR(R)ITYBREACH PA(E)PERCUTTER S(P)AFECRACKER LUCK(E)YBREAK GRAN(G)DOPENING And... all of those circled letters in sequence spelled out: SQUAREPEG Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=10/7/2018&h=106a Always nice to see something different. ....
I thought SUPE was the new name for A.I.

I entered DIRNDL for "Dress seen at Oktoberfest" while thinking, "If you think it's a dress and that's all you wear, you'll be picked up by the Polizei pretty quickly!"  But then I decided it's "dress" meaning "attire," which would have been more exact....  

I also had a moment with THE REST...at 52A.

Most Meh clue/entry:  Dance craze of the 2010's/DOUGIE.
Nevah heard of it!  Is it DEW-GHEE or DUG-ghee?  In that decade, both of our kids were entering their Thirty-somethings.
(Also, neither of our kids danced--one due to disability, the other due to "two left feet--one from each parent.")   
 Any of you guys do the DOUGIE?  Was it any fun?  (I remember when The Twist was all the rage, and back injuries were the result...)  

On with the week!

A quick Monday. I had to stare at the revealer for a moment or two before understanding dawned. 
Nonchalant/BLASE? Eh, I wouldn’t link the two meanings myself; the first being relaxed, the second unthinking/arrogant for me, but ok.

Liked it.  A cute theme, with no junk and intelligent fill.  Though if I were the Germans, I might sue.  They haven't been allowed to say anything but ACH since possibly the 1990s.  Well. at least here they're given Oktoberfest and the chance to wear a DIRNDL. Actually, you don't have to be German to wear a DIRNDL.  I first heard the word in a Harry Belafonte song from the 1950s.  I've always thought the song exceedingly beautiful, but I probably haven't listened to it for more than 65 years.  This time it made me cry.  I think you'll understand why.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dTL-fwRsEdc.  (If this doesn't come up in blue, the song's title is "Turn Around".)
I was on my way to a new best Monday time and got stuck on that dang German dress! 😂

I enjoyed the puzzle today! A fun theme too! 
But I'm completely lost on what the connection to the "to be or not to be..." quote is, can someone help? (As mentioned in the gameplay column). I'm sure it's obvious but I just can't think of it.

Had to run the alphabet to find the D in DOUGIE and DRINDLE but I’ve learned two things today. 
Nice to see our old friend ECRU make a cameo today. Haven’t seen it in a while and used to see it regularly.

One more puzzle find. This one quite remarkable. A Sunday from July 29, 1973 by Elmer Toro with the title: "Paintbox choices." Some theme clues and answers: "White" CLIFFSOFDOVERORWITHFURY "Red" ROSEOFTEXASORPAGES "Black" MAGICORKNIGHT "Gold" ILOCKSORSMITH "Pink" ELEPHANTORGIN "Purple" PEOPLEEATERORHEART Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/PS?date=7/29/1973 ....

Yeah, this is the wrong place for it (but I don't see anywhere else for this comment...) , but when is the NYTs going to fix the bug in the Midi puzzle?? 

For me and others I've talked to, when you start it  the screen says "nnn day streak", but when you've successfully completed it, it says "1 day streak"! That's been going on for a while now.

Having recently celebrated my German heritage at Oktoberfest, DIRNDL was a gimme for me. No, I do not own a pair of lederhosen, but I do own a jägerhut. (That's the hat that goes with the pants.)

No, I never did the DOUGIE, but I remember when it was a thing.

Today’s poem made from words in today’s puzzle…


a/ when i dreamed of the clouds in your mouth, i dreamed d/ the woods filled with a warning light
that you and i might see 
a/ the magic
Anyone else think the drag accessory was a bra? I couldn't even entertain another option and since it crosses German dress it did me in!

DIRNDL/DOUGIE had me guessing on a Monday. Not familiar with either entry, but chose the right letter and made it through this Monday(!) puzzle.

Seemed like a rough crossing there, especially for a Monday. But maybe that's just a reflection of my own ignorance.

DIRNDL has to be the most obscure word I've ever seen in a Monday puzzle. And as for TILT, that is hardly a "modern" innovation on pinball machines. Most tables since the 1960s have tilt alarms. Only the very oldest extant machines can be manhandled into cheating without a tilt, and you are only likely to see those in museums, not arcades.
DIRNDL on a Monday is a total power move.

The DIRNDL/DOUGIE was completely unnecessary for a Monday.

I can whine but accept it if it was a deliberate choice but if was just some random thing to complete the crossword when the setter was stuck at the section then this was really bad.

This feels surreal - for once my two gimmes of DIRNDL and BOA were stumpers for many 😃. So far it's always been the other way around!

Is *this* is what it's like to be a pro solver? 🤣

A note to remark on the cluing of FSTOP not adopting the convention of abbreviation matching, as I think f-stop is technically short for focal or focal length stop. But I guess f-number has been so thoroughly adopted in the language, or at least language of photography, to be a concept unto itself.
It's funny...I just happened to encounter DIRNDL a day or two ago in a Saturday archive puzzle. Did I commit the spelling to memory? Nope. Hence, an alphabet run on a Monday for _OUGIE 🤦🏼‍♀️

One more puzzle find. Not sure how one could possibly figure this one out (at least not me). Anyway - a Sunday from May 16, 1993 by Robert H. Wolfe with the title: "Genetic Jumble." Some theme clues and answers: "Clark's show?" AMERICNBDNASTDNA "Time piece?" GRDNAFATHERCLOCK And some other theme answers: MAGICWDNA HDNATOHDNACOMBAT LDNASCAPEGARDENER SDNAALWOODTREES ROWANDNAMARTINS And there were more. All of those were substituting DNA for AND, but I'm not sure what kind of chance anyone would have to figure that out. Here's the link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/PS?date=5/16/1993&h=85a ...
I got every single one. No help, except from crossers.  My mother was German so DIRNDL was easy, she made them for us as kids.

A few too many "sound" answers  (ACH, OHS,  AWS,  RAH...) to my taste today. 

I always feel as if the possible answers for "sound" clues are a little bit random and not particulary useful in helping me solve the puzzle -- though I am certain that they are very helpful to the puzzle maker when they are trying to a puzzle come together!  Though, as I think about it, maybe that's part of being a Monday puzzle - maybe sometimes the (presumably less experienced) maker of a Monday puzzle doesn't yet have the skills needed to avoid having to use such answers.
Got hardly any of the clues of the Midi ....

Worst Monday puzzle of all time and with a theme that made no sense. 

DIRNDL with DOUGIE Crosses and throw in LABORS for those not familiar with Hercules? Wow… Then throw in FTSOP. 

This was not fun.

Rating:
1/10
Very funny one! I had one mistake.
This was tough! DIRNDL, ELLE, DOUGIE, and LABORS (in this context) are all new to me, but somehow I got there, at 600% of my average Monday time :)

I suppose if we're looking from trends in the kinds of puzzles we're getting, the more obvious is that weekends are getting less difficult (sounds better than "easier").

But a concurrent trend, I think, is that early weeks are getting more difficult.  A lot of reports of running the alphabet in this one.  Personally, I'd gotten through Friday, Saturday, and Sunday without a single flyspec (I think), but I needed to make several changes in this one after I'd "finished". 

I wonder if The Great Easening is only one half of a phenomenon that is The Great Evening Up.

Did any of you have those old black-and-white "educational" films in elementary school.  With kids lined up and behaving ever so much better than actual kids in actual places?  (I particularly remember one little boy *cleaning his fingernails* before he went to school.  I rarely had time even to even get out of my pjs.

Anyway, in one of them there was a circle of kids asking the teacher about the meanings of words they'd heard.  

One little girl asked about a DIRNDL.  I almost laughed (even though I was a pretty repressed little kid) because it sounded so very stupid to me.  And I was shocked to find out it was a real word.

So DIRNDL didn't quite strike me as completely foreign, and I recall it as a little internal turbulence that I hadn't thought about for nearly three quarters of a century.  

But I still had trouble with the spelling.
This was really fun for a Monday.
For all those who didn’t know DIRNDL, i humbly submit that its place in Bavarian culture is rather akin to the cultural status of the beret in France. ie it’s not obscure.

I think it's entertaining that so many comments are about the word DIRNDL (and DOUGIE). Many people even comment that they ran the alphabet for this one. I definitely knew the word was DIRNdL but for some reason I just couldn't think of the right spelling. I, like others, had everything but the second "D." When I was in junior high school, I saw an ad in the back of "Seventeen" magazine for a lovely outfit. I guess it was a DIRNDL. It had a wide blue corduroy skirt with a very high tight waist and straps and a nice white blouse embroidered with blue flowers. I wore it for our class photo. So I definitely knew the word DIRNDL but just couldn't spit out the spelling for some reason. I clicked "Check Puzzle." So I got the "D." I also had a red diagonal line for SUPe. I had SUPT. That definitely was a typo, because I had previously added DOTIME. I also should have known SUPE because our superintendent was the king of our building all the time I was growing up. He seemed to have x-ray vision if one of us kids put one toe on the small lawn around our building! Then there he was, scolding us. Otherwise, I would have had the gold star! Here's a DIRNDL: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirndl
First time in ages I couldn’t finish a Monday puzzle because of the DOUGIE and DIRNDL cross. Have never heard of either and DIRNDL in the crossword is just evil.

I've been solving but not commenting, too busy with the campaigns, but had to check in on this cutie.  Tried to guess the revealer with no result so when that came into view - DOH!  A fun one this morning.

500th in line to say I also could not get DIRN*L/*OUGIE, I vaguely remember seeing the dress name before after plugging in random letters, but the dance craze completely passed me by. I'm not sure I've ever had to use guesswork to solve a Monday puzzle, so that's a feat for today's constructor.

This was rough, IMHO, for a Monday puzzle.  

While a DIRNDL might be culturally commonplace in Bavaria, it's not part of my vocabulary. Aside from that, I also have no clue about dance crazes, not forts in different states. 

While I got DIAN FOSSE?, I wasn't sure of the correct spelling.

All of thay made for a rough southeast corner that defeated me.

Once I was off my flight, I was able to cheat and solve the puzzle.
I thought the FSTOP - SUPE cross was a lot trickier than the DIRNDL - DOUGIE (though I knew dougie once a few letters were in) but fairly tricky for a Monday. ACT I also took me forever to figure out
If it weren’t for crosswords I’d never know the other definition of “at sea”. Aargh.

Fun! I share the columnist's gripe about phonetic letters, they always irrationally upset me in the puzzle. It feels ungodly to inflate a beautiful, lithe little S to ESS. That's twice the amount of S per S!

I'm amused by the different drag accessories listed in the comments; we though wig was a lock.
Ended a streak for me. Came here to see if others were similarly choked. My misery has found solance in company here.

Can we get some representation? Someone other than older white men writing these puzzles? As a trans woman, I couldn't help but immediately stop playing when I saw the answer to a drag performer's accessory. It's 2026, that's so deeply out of touch

Plug-in hybrids, of which the VOLT was one, are considered electric vehicles.

@Steve L

There is no strict definition of an EV (don't bother sending a Wikipedia reference). It's a matter of who you ask or where you look. 

The Cambridge Dictionary says it's "a type of vehicle that runs on electricity, usually one that does not use any other source of power.“ "Usually" is not strict.

@Elbridge Gerry

Compare
battery electric vehicle 
hybrid electric vehicle 
plug-in hybrid electric vehicle

And the definition of “hybrid electric vehicle”:

a vehicle that has both a gasoline engine and one or more electric motors:

And any site such as the one I cited previously, and there are several of them, which serve as primers on EVs, mention all three types of vehicles.

Ask the next person you know who has a hybrid if it's an electric vehicle. I'll bet they say no. Look for electric vehicles on autotrader - it will only show you teslas, Rivians and pure electrics. It depends on context.

I wouldn't call it outrage, but I paused a second at that clue/answer combo.  Not because it's a silly shortening, but because of the definition.

First of all, the only context I've ever heard SUPE as a superintendent was to refer to a school superintendent, which is a professional position, not a building custodian. In fact, it's a fairly high position, often the highest in the district.

The custodian of an apartment building in NY is also called a superintendent, but I've only heard it shortened to "super."  I guess I may not be keeping up with recent lingo, but it seems to me "super" should be pretty well entrenched by now so as not to need further alteration.

But my main point is that the supe(r) is not so much a building manager, which is to me someone who works in the rental office and manages the building's business, including scheduling work orders, as he (and it's practically always "he") is the custodian is the one who carries out those work orders and does the regular maintainance of the building, including cleaning common areas, upkeep of the mechanicals, etc.

Those to me are two separate positions, quite different from one another, but I realize that terminology might be different in other places (like Tasmania, apparently), so I didn't register a quibble.
